title: Linear Inequalities
prerequisites: Ability to solve linear equations in one variable.

topics.title: Solving Linear Inequalities in One Variable
topics.quick_summary: Linear inequalities are solved like equations, with one crucial exception: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
topics.real_life: A lift rated 'not more than 600 kg' defines an inequality, and every safety limit in engineering is written the same way.

detailed.definition: A strict inequality uses < or >; a slack inequality uses ≤ or ≥. The solution set is the set of all values of the variable satisfying the inequality.
detailed.key_idea: Adding or subtracting the same number leaves an inequality unchanged, and so does multiplying or dividing by a positive number. Only a negative multiplier flips the sign — that is the entire difference from equation solving.
detailed.working_principle: The solution of a linear inequality is generally an interval, not a single value, and is represented on the number line with a hollow circle for a strict inequality and a filled circle for a slack one.
applications: −3x > 12 gives x < −4 after dividing by −3 and reversing the sign.
Solution sets are written in interval notation, e.g. (−∞, −4).
Restricting the solution to integers or natural numbers changes the answer set.

points: Multiplying or dividing both sides by a NEGATIVE number reverses the inequality.
Adding or subtracting any number does not change the direction.
Strict inequality (<, >) is shown by a hollow circle on the number line.
Slack inequality (≤, ≥) is shown by a filled circle.
The solution is usually an interval containing infinitely many values.
mistakes: Forgetting to reverse the sign after dividing by a negative number.
Giving a single value as the answer instead of an interval.
Using a filled circle for a strict inequality.
topics.memory_hook: 'Negative flips it' — divide or multiply by a negative and the inequality turns around.
topics.advanced: Systems of linear inequalities define feasible regions in the plane, which is the foundation of linear programming. Optimising a linear objective over such a region always gives an answer at a corner of the region.
